# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## The Consensus Trap

There is a quiet ritual that plays out in conference rooms, video calls, and hallway conversations every day. A discussion winds down, someone looks around the table and asks, "So are we all aligned?" Heads nod. Someone types up notes that say the group "agreed to move forward." The meeting ends on a note of harmony, and everyone walks away feeling productive.

And yet, a week later, nothing has happened. Or worse: things have happened, but in three different directions, because it turns out the people who nodded were not actually thinking the same thing. The agreement was a mirage.

We tend to assume that a good meeting ends with everybody agreeing. This assumption is so deeply embedded in how we work that we rarely question it. But agreement can hide uncertainty. Two people can use the same words—"the launch is on track," "customers want this feature," "the vendor is reliable"—while holding entirely different pictures in their heads. When a group rushes to consensus, it often achieves nothing more than a temporary suppression of the differences that actually matter.
